name: Yara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights in the chilled section of a big grocery warehouse out on the ring road. I clock in at ten, put on the thermal jacket, grab a hand scanner and a pallet truck, and pick yoghurt, milk and cheese for the supermarkets until six. The scanner tells you where to go and counts your rate, and if you fall under it a team leader comes over with a printout. I'm still slow compared to the old hands, so I see that printout more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cold gets into your knuckles by three in the morning, and my back aches on the walk to the bus. What I like is the people on my shift, honestly. Rosa, our union rep, brings soup in a flask and we all share it at the four o'clock break. Sami, my partner, drives the early bus, so we pass each other at the door most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the robots were never the problem, the bosses are. If AI only speeds up the paperwork upstairs, nothing changes for us on the floor. I'd still post about the rate targets in the union group, because that fight doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not calm. My life was already tight before anyone said AI. The rate keeps going up every spring and I'm one of the slow ones, so I'm always one bad month from being moved to fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights and try to get my pick rate up so they stop picking on me. I'd stop the takeaway on Fridays to put maybe 30 a month aside. And I'd go to every union meeting, because Rosa says the new contract talks start next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Like the world gets to stay the same, and the same is already hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you already get the printout about your rate. What's the money like right now, month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent eats more than half of what Sami and I bring in. I've got less than a month saved, and the boiler in our flat is on its last legs. If my hours dropped even by one night a week, we'd be choosing between the phone bill and the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first if the hours did get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, before anyone. She's been there eleven years and she knows which managers you can talk to. Then my mum, but my mum hasn't got money to give, only advice I don't want.

say: Robots and AI were never the real problem; the **bosses** and **rate targets** are.
I'll keep posting about the **pick-rate targets** in the union group, because that fight goes on regardless.
think: I'm relieved, but my life was **already tight** before anyone mentioned AI.
I'm one of the **slow pickers**, so one bad month could mean fewer shifts.
do: Keep working **night shifts** and push my pick rate up so team leaders stop printing warnings.
Cut the Friday takeaway to **save about 30** a month.
Go to every **union meeting** before next year's contract talks.
feel: **Tired**, because staying the same still means staying stretched.
Slightly **relieved** that nothing new is coming for the job.
S0.quote: I've got less than a month saved, and the boiler in our flat is on its last legs.
fieldNote: Her **money worry** exists without AI: rent takes over half the household income and savings are under a month.
She blames **management targets**, not technology, and sees the union as her only real lever.
Her **pick rate** is below average, which makes her the first in line for lost shifts.

steps.text: Keep working chilled-section night shifts and raise her pick rate
Drop Friday takeaway to put aside about 30 a month
Attend every union meeting before next year's contract talks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing louder: the company will use this to squeeze us, not to make our lives easier. At work I'd tell people to join the union now, before it starts, not after. Online I'd share anything that shows the profits going up while the rota shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking stuff doesn't touch my hands, but it touches the people who decide my shifts. If a computer plans the rota and the rate, it won't care that I'm slow because I'm still learning. And once they see robots can move a pallet, they'll start testing them in our aisles too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the extra Saturday shifts while they're there, to build a bit of cushion. I'd ask Rosa to get me onto the union's training for workplace reps, because I'd rather be in the room. I wouldn't touch the AI apps myself, I don't trust them with anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is getting slippery and nobody will say it out loud. My stomach knots up just thinking about the rota coming out on a Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the managers' computers. Has anything like that already shown up at your warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, last year the new planning software started telling team leaders how many pickers to bring in. They cut two agency lads the first week. Nobody explained it, the screen just said fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ken in ambient, who's fifty-nine and can't learn a new scanner to save his life. And me, really, because I'm in the same boat as him, just younger.

say: The company will use AI to **squeeze workers**, not to make our lives easier.
Everyone should **join the union** now, before the changes start rather than after.
think: AI won't touch my hands, but it will decide my **shifts and rate**.
Once robots prove they can move pallets, they'll start **testing them** in our aisles.
do: Take **extra Saturday shifts** while they're still offered to build a small cushion.
Ask Rosa to get me onto the **union rep training**.
Avoid the **AI apps** myself, because I don't trust them.
feel: **Knotted up**, especially when the weekly rota comes out on Thursday.
Like the ground is getting **slippery** and nobody says it.
S1.quote: Last year the new planning software started telling team leaders how many pickers to bring in. They cut two agency lads the first week.
fieldNote: She has already seen **planning software** cut agency workers, so this scenario feels real, not hypothetical.
Her response is **collective**: become a rep, get in the room, rather than learn the tools.
She ties her fate to an **older colleague**, seeing both as people software won't wait for.

steps.text: Take extra Saturday shifts while offered and keep that money aside
Sign up for the union's workplace rep training through Rosa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be out on the street with a sign, I'm not joking. I'd say governments let this happen, and they owe people like me a wage while it sorts itself out. In the group chat I'd be the one saying don't wait, organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I lose this job, maybe not in 2028 but by 2031 for sure. I've got no qualifications, I left school early, and there's only two other warehouses within a bus ride. I don't know what I'd be for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and keep the job as long as it lasts, and push the union for a deal on redundancy pay. I'd write to our local MP with the others, every week if needed. Sami and I would move in with his sister to cut the rent by half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, like a dream where you're late and can't find the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the office side changes in 2028 but the robots come around 2031. What happens in those three years for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years would be the worst bit, because everyone would know what's coming. The office would get leaner, the rates would get stricter, and they'd stop hiring. I'd hang on and hope the union wins something before the robots roll in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat first, it's the biggest bill. Then the gym Sami pays for, and my phone contract. I'd rather lose a room than lose the job, but I'd probably lose both.

say: **Governments** let this happen and owe people like me a **wage** while it settles.
I'd tell everyone in the group chat to **organise now**, not wait and see.
think: I lose this job, maybe not in 2028 but **by 2031** for sure.
With **no qualifications** and two other warehouses nearby, I don't know what I'd become.
do: Stay in the job as long as possible and push the union for **redundancy pay**.
Write to our **local MP** with colleagues every week if needed.
Move in with **Sami's sister** to halve our rent.
feel: **Scared**, like a dream where you're late and can't find the door.
S2.quote: I've got no qualifications, I left school early, and there's only two other warehouses within a bus ride. I don't know what I'd be for.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** before robots as a squeeze, not breathing room: stricter rates and frozen hiring.
Her plan is **political and collective**, with no personal retraining at all.
She'd give up **the flat** before the job, showing how little room she has.

steps.text: Push the union for a redundancy pay deal before robots arrive
Write weekly to the local MP with colleagues from her shift
Move in with Sami's sister to halve the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, just with more time to fight. I'd be saying make the companies pay a tax on every robot and give it to the people they replace. I'd say it at work, at the pub and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years buys me time, not safety. I'd still be the slow picker in a warehouse that's counting down to robots. I'm 27 now, I'd be 34 or 35 when the hands-on side goes, which is no age to start from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly, even 50 a month, so we're not at zero when it hits. I'd get more involved in the union, maybe stand as a rep. Sami would keep the bus job, and I'd ask him to look at whether the bus company still needs drivers by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a box that keeps getting heavier while you walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years gives you time to fight. What does a win look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A win is a law that says if you bring robots in, you keep people on full pay for a year and retrain them. Rosa says that's a dream, but every good thing was a dream once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that would try a different line of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe care work, like my auntie does. People will still want a human hand when they're old. But I'm not good with change, I'd be terrified of starting over somewhere new.

say: Companies should pay a **tax on every robot** and give it to replaced workers.
I'd say that at work, at the pub and online, wherever people listen.
think: Five years buys me **time, not safety**; I'm still the slow picker.
I'd be **34 or 35** when hands-on work goes, which is late to restart.
do: Save **50 a month**, so we're not at zero when it hits.
Stand as a **union rep** and push for a year of paid retraining.
Ask Sami to check whether the **bus company** still needs drivers.
feel: **Heavy**, like a box that keeps getting heavier while I walk.
S3.quote: I'm 27 now, I'd be 34 or 35 when the hands-on side goes, which is no age to start from nothing.
fieldNote: Extra years turn into **saving and organising**, not a career change.
She floats **care work** like her auntie's, then backs away from the fear of starting over.
She leans on **Sami's bus job** as the household's safer income.

steps.text: Set aside 50 a month from her night-shift pay
Stand as a union rep and push for paid retraining
Rely on Sami's bus-driving pay if her hours go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, at least there's time to get the rules right. Ten years is long enough for a government to actually do something if people push. I'd tell the young ones at work to join the union and stay loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably feel a bit easier, if I'm honest. By the time robots can do my job I'd be nearly 40, and maybe I'd have moved off nights by then. But I'd still be someone with no papers and no savings, so it's only easier, not easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and finally do the forklift course the union offers for free, because forklifts might last a bit longer than pickers. I'd save what I can, and I'd keep pushing the union on the robot-tax idea. I wouldn't change more than that, I'm not a jump-first person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick to my stomach. Still worried, but it feels like something I can walk towards slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you want to have done by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have a bit of money saved, a forklift licence, and maybe be on days instead of nights. Sami and I talk about kids someday, and I'd want to know I can feed them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sami say about that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami would say go for it, he always does. My partner Sami also knows I'll talk myself out of the forklift course three times before I sign up.

say: Ten years is enough for **governments to act**, if workers keep pushing.
I'd tell the young ones at work to **join the union** and stay loud.
think: I'd be nearly **40** when robots arrive, possibly off nights by then.
With **no papers** and no savings, it's only easier, not easy.
do: Take the union's **free forklift course**, since forklifts may outlast pickers.
Keep saving what I can and pushing the union's **robot-tax** idea.
feel: **Less sick** to my stomach, though still worried.
Like something I can **walk towards** slowly rather than run from.
S4.quote: My partner Sami also knows I'll talk myself out of the forklift course three times before I sign up.
fieldNote: The ten-year window lets her consider a **small skill step**, the forklift licence, for the first time.
She knows she **resists change** and expects to talk herself out of it.
Future **children** come up only here, once there is time to plan.

steps.text: Sign up for the union's free forklift licence course
Keep saving a little each month from her pay
Keep pushing the union to campaign for a robot tax

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years is nothing when you've got under a month in the bank and no qualifications. What would help is a law that makes them keep us on and pay for retraining, and a union strong enough to make it stick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people like me what we'd want to do instead. Nobody ever asks the pickers. I don't know my answer yet, but I'd like to be asked before the robots arrive, not after.

headlineQuote: Nobody ever asks the pickers. I don't know my answer yet, but I'd like to be asked before the robots arrive, not after.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old picker** on night shift in a chilled grocery warehouse, still slower than the target rate.
She has **under a month** saved, shares rent with Sami, a bus driver, and few warehouses are nearby.
She blames **bosses and governments**, not machines, and her answer to every scenario is the union.
She avoids **AI tools** and new things, and only considers a forklift course when given ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is nothing with no savings and no qualifications.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** forcing firms to keep workers on and pay for **retraining**.
A **union** strong enough to make that law stick.
